interactions.label: A 55-year-old cotton mill worker presents with chest tightness that is worst on

params.question: A 55-year-old cotton mill worker presents with chest tightness that is worst on Monday morning and improves by midweek. Which occupational lung disease is most consistent with this pattern?

answers.text: Silicosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Silicosis presents with progressive breathlessness and upper-zone nodular opacities after prolonged silica exposure, without any characteristic weekly variation in symptoms.

answers.text: Byssinosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Byssinosis classically causes symptoms worst on Monday ('Monday fever') that ease as the week progresses, due to cotton or textile dust exposure. Early disease is reversible, but chronic exposure leads to fixed airway obstruction.

answers.text: Asbestosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Asbestosis causes lower-zone fibrosis and calcified pleural plaques. Its feared complications include mesothelioma and lung cancer, but it does not show the Monday worsening pattern.

answers.text: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CWP produces upper-zone small nodules and may progress to massive fibrosis, but it follows a chronic progressive course without weekly symptom fluctuation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Monday worsening pattern is the hallmark of byssinosis from cotton dust exposure. Unlike silicosis, asbestosis, or CWP, early byssinosis is reversible — making occupational history crucial for timely diagnosis.
Exactly right. The Monday worsening pattern is pathognomonic of byssinosis and distinguishes it from the other pneumoconioses, which follow a steadily progressive course.

interactions.label: A rubber factory uses benzene as a solvent. Workers are provided respirators, bu

params.question: A rubber factory uses benzene as a solvent. Workers are provided respirators, but exposure monitoring still shows levels above the threshold limit value. Which single intervention from the hierarchy of controls would be MOST effective?

answers.text: Providing better-fitting respirators

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Upgrading PPE is the lowest tier of the hierarchy. PPE does not reduce the hazard itself and depends entirely on consistent, correct use by each worker.

answers.text: Rotating workers to limit individual exposure time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Job rotation is an administrative control, ranked below elimination, substitution, and engineering controls. It limits each worker's dose but does not remove or replace the hazard.

answers.text: Substituting benzene with toluene

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Substitution replaces the hazardous agent with a safer alternative — toluene is far less leukaemogenic than benzene. This sits near the top of the hierarchy, well above administrative controls or PPE.

answers.text: Installing warning signs about benzene hazards

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warning signs are an administrative control and one of the least effective tiers. They rely on worker awareness without reducing the actual hazard level in the workplace.

overallFeedback.feedback: Substitution — replacing benzene with toluene — is the most effective feasible option here. The hierarchy ranks elimination and substitution above engineering, administrative, and PPE measures because higher tiers reduce reliance on worker behaviour.
Well done. Substitution ranks near the top of the hierarchy because it removes the specific hazard at source, unlike administrative controls or PPE which rely on worker behaviour.

interactions.label: Which of the following correctly describes the Employees' State Insurance (ESI)

params.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) scheme in India?

answers.text: It is a voluntary insurance scheme available to all Indian workers regardless of sector

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ESI scheme is compulsory, not voluntary, and applies specifically to workers in factories and notified establishments — not to all workers across sectors.

answers.text: It is a compulsory, contributory scheme providing medical care and cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disability, and death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ESI Act 1948 established a compulsory scheme with contributions from both employer and employee. ESIC, under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, administers comprehensive medical and cash benefits.

answers.text: It covers only workplace injuries and does not include medical treatment for diseases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ESI scheme is comprehensive — it provides full medical care along with cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disability, and dependants, not just injury compensation.

answers.text: It is administered by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ESIC is a statutory body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, not the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. This placement reflects its identity as a labour welfare measure.

overallFeedback.feedback: The ESI scheme is a compulsory, contributory insurance programme run by ESIC under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It provides medical care plus cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disability, and death — a comprehensive welfare framework, not limited to injuries alone.
Correct. The ESI scheme is India's primary social security measure for organised sector workers, combining contributory insurance with comprehensive health and cash benefits.

interactions.label: Despite their high prevalence, occupational disorders among healthcare workers a

params.question: Despite their high prevalence, occupational disorders among healthcare workers are often under-recognised. Which combination of factors best explains this gap?

answers.text: Low actual incidence of workplace injuries in healthcare settings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Healthcare is one of the highest-risk occupations — with approximately 2 million needlestick injuries annually and back injury rates among the highest of any profession. Incidence is not low; recognition is.

answers.text: Cultural stoicism, stigma around bloodborne exposures, and absent occupational health services in most hospitals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Healthcare workers often do not report injuries due to normalised stoicism, fear of stigma (especially around needlestick and bloodborne exposures), and the lack of occupational health services in most district-level facilities.

answers.text: Legal exemptions that exclude healthcare workers from occupational health reporting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no legal exemption for healthcare workers. The under-recognition stems from cultural and systemic barriers within healthcare institutions, not from any regulatory provision.

answers.text: Effective institutional programmes that prevent most injuries before they occur

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Most healthcare facilities, particularly in low-resource settings, lack any formal occupational health programme. The recognition gap exists precisely because protective systems are absent, not because they are effective.

overallFeedback.feedback: Under-recognition is driven by a culture of stoicism, stigma around bloodborne exposures, weak institutional reporting, and the near-total absence of occupational health services in most Indian hospitals. Healthcare workers often end up managing their own injuries poorly or not at all.
Exactly. Recognising these systemic barriers — stoicism, stigma, and absent services — is the first step towards building effective occupational health programmes for healthcare workers.

interactions.label: An anaesthesiologist working in an operation theatre without a gas scavenging sy

params.question: An anaesthesiologist working in an operation theatre without a gas scavenging system reports chronic fatigue and tingling in the extremities. Which mechanism best explains these symptoms?

answers.text: Direct hepatotoxicity from halogenated anaesthetic agents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While halogenated agents can cause liver injury, the combination of fatigue and peripheral tingling points to a haematological and neurological mechanism — specifically, impaired vitamin B₁₂ metabolism from chronic N₂O exposure.

answers.text: Irreversible inactivation of methionine synthase by nitrous oxide, impairing vitamin B₁₂ metabolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Chronic N₂O exposure irreversibly inactivates methionine synthase, disrupting B₁₂-dependent DNA synthesis. This causes megaloblastic anaemia (fatigue) and peripheral neuropathy (tingling) — both preventable with proper scavenging systems.

answers.text: Type I hypersensitivity to latex proteins in surgical gloves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Latex allergy typically presents as urticaria, contact dermatitis, or anaphylaxis — not chronic fatigue with neuropathy. The occupational history here points clearly to waste anaesthetic gas exposure.

answers.text: Cumulative ionising radiation from fluoroscopy-guided procedures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radiation exposure causes deterministic effects (skin changes, cataracts) or stochastic effects (cancer risk), not the fatigue-plus-neuropathy pattern described here. This clinical picture fits N₂O toxicity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Chronic N₂O exposure irreversibly inactivates methionine synthase, blocking vitamin B₁₂ metabolism. The downstream effects — megaloblastic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy — explain both the fatigue and the tingling. Proper gas scavenging systems are the primary prevention measure.
Well reasoned. N₂O's irreversible inactivation of methionine synthase is the key mechanism — explaining both the haematological and neurological effects of chronic operating theatre exposure.

interactions.label: A second-year surgical resident reports feeling emotionally drained, increasingl

params.question: A second-year surgical resident reports feeling emotionally drained, increasingly cynical towards patients, and doubts whether their work makes any difference. Using the Maslach Burnout Inventory framework, how many of its three dimensions does this presentation fulfil?

answers.text: One — emotional exhaustion only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The resident's cynicism towards patients reflects depersonalisation (dimension two), and doubting one's impact reflects reduced personal accomplishment (dimension three). All three MBI dimensions are present here.

answers.text: Two — emotional exhaustion and depersonalisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 'Doubts whether their work makes any difference' maps directly to the third MBI dimension — reduced personal accomplishment. All three dimensions are present, not just two.

answers.text: Three — emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and reduced personal accomplishment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. 'Emotionally drained' = emotional exhaustion; 'cynical towards patients' = depersonalisation; 'doubts whether their work makes any difference' = reduced personal accomplishment. This is the classic complete burnout profile.

answers.text: Two — depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 'Emotionally drained' maps directly to emotional exhaustion, the first MBI dimension. All three dimensions are present, constituting complete burnout — not a partial syndrome.

overallFeedback.feedback: All three Maslach Burnout Inventory dimensions are present: emotional exhaustion ('emotionally drained'), depersonalisation ('cynical towards patients'), and reduced personal accomplishment ('doubts whether work makes a difference'). This constitutes the classic burnout profile described in the video.
Exactly right. Recognising all three MBI dimensions in a clinical presentation identifies complete burnout — prompting institutional intervention rather than treating it as personal weakness.
